corpus_definition: The work of putting together the parts to make something large.

forms.definition: the work of building things like houses, roads and bridges
forms.example: The construction of the new metro station in Tashkent took three years.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning: 'building work'.
Common British phrase for this kind of work.
Related: new houses or offices being planned and built in an area.

ant.note: Demolition is the work of knocking a building down.

forms.definition: to build something such as a house, road or bridge
forms.example: The company plans to construct a new bridge over the river.

syn.note: Easy everyday word; construct is more formal.
Informal: used for buildings, walls and tents.
Very formal, used for buildings and statues.
General easy word; construct is for large things with many parts.

ant.note: To knock a building down completely.
Informal: to destroy a building or wall.

forms.definition: helpful and meant to make something better
forms.example: My teacher gave me some constructive advice about my essay.
forms.note: Belongs to construct = build something good (ideas, criticism), not building houses.

forms.definition: in a helpful way that improves something
forms.example: Let's talk constructively about how to fix the problem.
forms.note: Goes with constructive = helpful, not building houses.

people.definition: a person or company that builds things such as roads or houses
people.example: The constructor finished the school before September.
people.note: Less common than builder; also used for a company that builds racing cars.

context.text: There is a lot of construction in our city this year. Workers are constructing new apartment blocks near the park, so the streets are noisy.

reviewer_note: Trap: constructive/constructively mean 'helpful', so they are other_meaning, not 'about building'.

corpus_definition: To talk or write to someone to share news.

forms.definition: communication with someone by phone, letter, email or meeting
forms.example: We have stayed in contact since we left school.
forms.note: Common phrases: 'in contact with', 'make contact', 'lose contact'. A contact can also be a person you know who can help you.

syn.note: Used in fixed phrases: 'stay in touch', 'get in touch'; more informal.
More formal and general.
Related: a link between people or things.

forms.definition: to call, write to or email someone to give or get news
forms.example: Please contact me if you need help.
forms.note: No preposition after the verb: say 'contact me', not 'contact to me' or 'contact with me'.

syn.note: Very close and a little less formal.
Often about managing to talk to someone: 'I couldn't reach him.'
Only by phone.
Only by letter, email or message.
Only by email.

forms.note: There is no common adjective in this family. Contactable (easy to reach by phone or email) is rare.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: If you have any questions, contact our office in Samarkand. We try to stay in contact with every student after the course.

reviewer_note: Uzbek/Russian speakers often add 'with' or 'to' after the verb; noted. Contactable left as rare.

corpus_definition: To have something inside as part of it.

forms.definition: the things that are inside a box, bag, room or other thing
forms.example: The contents of my bag fell out onto the floor.
forms.note: Usually plural in this meaning: the contents of a box, bag or bottle. Stress: CONtent. (conTENT = happy is a different word.)

syn.note: Related: only about the things in food or a recipe.

forms.definition: the act of keeping something harmful under control
forms.example: The containment of the fire took the whole night.
forms.note: Belongs to contain = keep something under control (a fire, a disease), not having something inside.

forms.definition: to have something inside or as a part
forms.example: This box does not contain any plastic.
forms.note: Not used in continuous tenses: say 'it contains', not 'it is containing'.

syn.note: Easy word, often about how much something can have inside: 'The bottle holds one litre.'
Used when something is one part of a group or list.
Very general easy word.
Related: tells you ALL the parts, not just some.

ant.note: To leave something out so it is not a part.

forms.note: There is no adjective in this meaning. Content (= happy, satisfied), continent and continental share an old Latin root with contain but are not made from it.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a box, bottle or similar thing that you keep things in
people.example: Put the leftover plov in a plastic container.

context.text: This juice contains a lot of sugar. Always read the label to check the contents before you buy it, then keep it in a glass container in the fridge.

reviewer_note: Noun content(s) = the things inside is this meaning; containment is the 'control' meaning (other_meaning). Content (= satisfied) and continent share the old root but are not made from contain (not_family).

corpus_definition: A formal written agreement between two or more people or groups.

forms.definition: a formal written agreement that people or companies sign
forms.example: They signed a new contract yesterday.
forms.note: Phrases: sign a contract, break a contract, a one-year contract.

syn.note: Easy and general; a contract is a legal, written agreement.
Informal: an arrangement, often about business or money.
Related: any official paper, not only an agreement.

forms.definition: the process of becoming smaller or shorter
forms.example: The contraction of the metal happens when it gets cold.
forms.note: Belongs to contract = become smaller (a verb meaning), not a legal agreement. In grammar, a contraction is a short form like 'don't'.

forms.definition: to make a formal agreement for someone to do work
forms.example: The city contracted a local company to repair the roads.
forms.note: The verb also means 'become smaller' and 'catch an illness'; those are other meanings. Stress: noun CONtract, verb conTRACT.

syn.note: Easier and more general: to pay someone to do work.
Usually about a long-term job, not one piece of work.

forms.definition: agreed in or connected with a formal written agreement
forms.example: The company has a contractual duty to finish the work on time.

syn.note: Related: connected with the law.
Related: something you must legally do.

forms.definition: in a way that is agreed in a formal written agreement
forms.example: The builders are contractually required to finish by May.

syn.note: Related: in a way connected with the law.

people.definition: a person or company that is paid to do work, often building
people.example: We hired a contractor to build the new kitchen.

context.text: My brother got a two-year contract with a building contractor in Tashkent. He is contractually allowed four weeks of holiday each year.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR B1). contraction (become smaller) kept as other_meaning; no -al affix claimed on contractual (contractu- is not a word).

gate_overrides.reason: contraction is contract + the suffix -ion (a derivation, like construction), not a compound of two words; it is the 'become smaller' meaning, kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To deal successfully with a difficult situation.

forms.note: There is no common noun in this family. Coping is used in phrases like 'coping skills'.

forms.definition: to manage a difficult situation or problem successfully
forms.example: It is hard to cope with so much work.
forms.note: Usually 'cope with + noun'. Also used alone: 'I can't cope!'

syn.note: Easy and very close: 'I can manage.'
Common phrase; often about taking action to solve a problem.
Close; often about a person, task or situation.
Informal: to have just enough money or help to live.
Related: stronger, about staying alive or getting through something very hard.

ant.note: To have great difficulty with something instead of managing it well.

forms.note: There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: In her first year at university in Tashkent, Malika found it hard to cope with all the homework. Now she copes much better because she plans her week.

reviewer_note: Only the verb exists in this family; 'coping' (noun, part of a wall) is a different word.

corpus_definition: A soft reddish metal used for electricity wires.

forms.definition: a soft reddish-brown metal used for wires and pipes
forms.example: The coins were made of copper and silver.

syn.note: Related: a brown metal made from this metal and tin.
Related: a yellow metal made from this metal and zinc.
General easy word for iron, gold, silver and similar materials.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: made of the soft reddish-brown metal, or having its colour
forms.example: My grandmother cooks plov in a big copper pot.
forms.note: Used before a noun: copper wire, copper pot, copper hair.

syn.note: Only about the colour.
Means 'like this metal', usually about colour; less common.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: In the old bazaar in Bukhara, men still make copper plates by hand. The copper bowls shine red in the sun.

reviewer_note: Copper (informal British = police officer) comes from 'cop', a different word, so it is not shown.

corpus_definition: A change that makes something right.

forms.definition: a change that makes something right or fixes a mistake
forms.example: I need to make a small correction here.

syn.note: Informal: a way of solving a problem.
General easy word; a correction is a change that removes a mistake.
Formal: a small change to a law, document or text.
A change after you check something again, often to a text.

ant.note: More formal word for a mistake.

forms.definition: the quality of being right or accurate
forms.example: The teacher checks the correctness of every answer.

syn.note: Very close; often about numbers and facts.
Related: being exact in every detail.

forms.definition: to make something right by finding and fixing mistakes
forms.example: Our teacher corrects our homework every evening.

syn.note: Easy, informal word.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.
British: what teachers do to students' work.
Formal: to change a text or law.
To change a text to make it better.

forms.definition: right, true, or with no mistakes
forms.example: All your answers are correct.

syn.note: Easy everyday word.
Exact and true, often about numbers or facts.
About facts and statements.

forms.definition: meant to make something better or right
forms.example: He wears corrective glasses for reading.

forms.definition: in a right way, without any mistakes
forms.example: Make sure you spell your name correctly on the form.

syn.note: Informal: 'Did I do it right?'
In the way it should be done.
Exactly and with no mistakes.

ant.note: In a way that is not right.

context.text: Please check that all the dates are correct. If you find a mistake, write the correction in red and send it back to me so I can correct the list.

reviewer_note: Headword is the noun; the verb and adjective 'correct' are the base of the family.

forms.definition: the feeling of being warm, comfortable and relaxed
forms.example: I love the coziness of my grandmother's kitchen in winter.
forms.note: British spelling: cosiness.

syn.note: A more general easy word.
Related: about heat or friendly feelings.

ant.note: A feeling of not being comfortable.

forms.note: There is no single-word verb in this meaning. The phrasal verb 'cozy up (to)' means to move close to someone or to be friendly to get something.

forms.definition: warm, comfortable and pleasant, making you feel relaxed
forms.example: We sat by the fire in the cozy room.
forms.note: American spelling: cozy. British spelling: cosy.

syn.note: Very close; often about a small warm place.
Easy, general word; cozy also means warm and friendly.
Only about temperature or friendly feelings.
American English; British English says 'homely'.

ant.note: Not pleasant to be in or sit in.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family. Cozily (BrE cosily) is rare.

context.text: Our little flat in Fergana is cozy in winter. In the evening we drink tea under a warm blanket and enjoy the coziness.

reviewer_note: US/UK spelling noted (cozy/cosy). Cozily treated as rare.

corpus_definition: a thin line that appears when something is damaged or broken

forms.definition: a thin line on a surface where it has started to break
forms.example: There is a small crack in the glass.

syn.note: A long line where something has broken open, often wood or cloth.
Formal or medical: a crack in a bone or hard material.
Related: an empty space between two things.
Related: a small piece broken off the edge.

forms.definition: to break so that thin lines appear on the surface
forms.example: The old plate cracked when I washed it in hot water.

syn.note: General easy word; crack means it doesn't break into pieces.
To break along a line.
Formal or medical: used for bones.

forms.definition: to make many short sharp sounds
forms.example: The wood crackled in the fire.
forms.note: Belongs to crack = a sharp noise, not a thin line.

forms.definition: having thin lines on it because it is damaged
forms.example: Don't drink from that cracked cup.

syn.note: General easy word; broken can mean in pieces.
General word for any kind of harm.
With a small piece broken off.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a thin, dry, hard biscuit, often eaten with cheese
people.example: We had crackers and cheese for a snack.
people.note: Belongs to crack = break with a sharp sound, not a thin line.

context.text: After the earthquake there was a long crack in the wall of our school. The walls had cracked in many places, so builders came to repair them.

reviewer_note: crack also has meanings like 'a sharp noise' and 'solve a problem'; crackle and cracker kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A bad accident involving a moving vehicle.

forms.definition: an accident in which a car, bus or plane hits something
forms.example: The car was damaged in the crash.

syn.note: Easy and more general; a crash is a violent one.
Formal: when two things hit each other.
Informal British English for a bad car accident.
American English: a crash, or the broken car or plane after it.

forms.definition: to have an accident by hitting something hard while moving
forms.example: The bus crashed into a tree on the way to Namangan.

syn.note: Formal: two things hit each other.
General easy word.
Informal and strong: hit very hard.
Hit something with your car, often not very hard.

forms.definition: done very quickly and with a lot of effort
forms.example: I did a crash course in English before my trip.
forms.note: Belongs to crash = sudden and fast, not an accident. Used only before a noun: a crash course, a crash diet.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: There was a bad crash on the road to Samarkand last night. A truck crashed into two cars, but luckily nobody died.

reviewer_note: Adjective 'crash' (crash course) kept as other_meaning; computer 'crash' and money 'crash' are other meanings not shown.
